This report reads {{< var n_postings >}} open, senior-eligible postings from {{< var n_companies >}} employers,
fetched on {{< var fetched >}}, and counts which of {{< var n_skills >}} skills each one names. The skills are
grouped into {{< var n_areas >}} areas. Every skill listed here has review questions on the
[skill pages](../skills/index.qmd) and in the [review app](../review/index.qmd).

Percentages are the share of postings whose description names the skill. A posting names a skill when its
text matches that skill's patterns in `tools/taxonomy.py`; the [method and limits](#method) section says what
that does and does not measure.

## Summary

- **Three different jobs share these titles.** Machine learning engineer postings ask for PyTorch
  ({{< var p_pytorch_mle >}}%), the path to production ({{< var p_production_ml_mle >}}%) and MLOps
  ({{< var p_mlops_mle >}}%). AI engineer postings ask for agents ({{< var p_agents_ai >}}%), agent frameworks
  and harnesses ({{< var p_orchestration_ai >}}%), backend services ({{< var p_backend_ai >}}%) and
  TypeScript ({{< var p_typescript_ai >}}%), and only {{< var p_pytorch_ai >}}% name PyTorch. Research engineer
  postings ask for experiment rigor ({{< var p_experimentation_re >}}%), fast and correct research code
  ({{< var p_research_eng_re >}}%) and reinforcement learning ({{< var p_rl_re >}}%).
- **LLMs are the default subject.** {{< var p_llm_general >}}% of all postings name LLMs or foundation models and
  {{< var p_agents >}}% name agents. Classical ML is named far less often: classical models in
  {{< var p_classical_ml >}}%, feature engineering in {{< var p_feature_eng >}}%, statistics in
  {{< var p_statistics >}}%.
- **Evaluation is the technical skill the three tracks share most evenly.** {{< var p_evals >}}% of postings
  name model evaluation ({{< var p_evals_mle >}}%, {{< var p_evals_ai >}}% and {{< var p_evals_re >}}% by track),
  and {{< var p_llm_evals >}}% name eval harnesses, judges or graders specifically.
- **Production comes before modelling.** Shipping to production ({{< var p_production_ml >}}%), reliability
  ({{< var p_reliability >}}%), latency and throughput ({{< var p_latency >}}%) and monitoring
  ({{< var p_ml_observability >}}%) are each named more often than PyTorch ({{< var p_pytorch >}}%) or any
  training method (fine-tuning: {{< var p_finetuning >}}%).
- **Senior means scope.** Ownership is named in {{< var p_ownership >}}% of postings, cross-functional work in
  {{< var p_xfn >}}%, communication in {{< var p_communication >}}%, ambiguity in {{< var p_ambiguity >}}%. Technical
  leadership rises from {{< var lv_tech_leadership_senior >}}% of postings titled senior to
  {{< var lv_tech_leadership_principal >}}% of those titled principal.
- **Working with AI coding agents is now a named skill**: {{< var p_ai_coding_tools >}}% of postings overall and
  {{< var p_ai_coding_tools_ai >}}% of AI engineer postings.
- **Experience asked**: {{< var yoe_share >}}% of postings state a number of years; the median is
  {{< var yoe_median >}}, and {{< var yoe_staff >}} for postings titled staff.
- **What postings leave out**: only {{< var p_dsa >}}% mention data structures and algorithms, yet nearly every
  loop has a coding round. Section [What interviews test beyond the posting](#loops) maps the rounds to the areas.

## What was collected

Postings come from the public job-board feeds of Greenhouse, Ashby and Lever for a list of AI labs, AI product
startups, AI infrastructure companies, consumer and marketplace technology companies, robotics and autonomy
companies and trading firms, plus the career sites of large employers that run their own
(`tools/fetch_jobs.py`, `tools/fetch_jobs_bigtech.py`). A posting is kept when its title is a machine learning
engineer, AI engineer or research engineer role (including "software engineer, ML" and "member of technical
staff" with an ML subject), is not an internship, new-graduate, management, sales or hardware role, and its
description names at least three ML skills.

The feeds returned {{< var n_raw >}} matching postings, {{< var n_unique >}} after merging the same role posted
in several locations. {{< var dropped_not_ml >}} were dropped because the description names fewer than three ML
skills and {{< var dropped_junior >}} because the title or the experience asked is below senior, leaving
{{< var n_postings >}}. {{< var us_share >}}% list a United States location. The largest employers are capped at
150 postings each so that no one company dominates.

## The three tracks

The same title words cover different work. The tables below show, for each track, the skills that separate it
most from the other two, then its top 25 technical skills.

### Machine learning engineer

The MLE postings are about training models and running them in production: PyTorch, MLOps, model serving,
distributed training, metrics. This track also holds the two specialised families, search / recommendation /
ads and autonomy / robotics, each with its own vocabulary.

{{< include _gen/distinct_mle.md >}}

<details class="qa"><summary>Top 25 technical skills in MLE postings</summary>

{{< include _gen/track_mle.md >}}

</details>

### AI engineer

The AI engineer postings describe software engineers who build products on top of models: agents, tools,
retrieval, evaluation, and the backend and frontend around them. Model training is rare here; reliability,
cloud and developer tooling are common. {{< var n_arch_forward_deployed >}} postings in the sample are
forward-deployed roles that sit with a customer.

{{< include _gen/distinct_ai-engineer.md >}}

<details class="qa"><summary>Top 25 technical skills in AI engineer postings</summary>

{{< include _gen/track_ai-engineer.md >}}

</details>

### Research engineer

The research engineer postings describe engineers inside research teams: they build training and evaluation
systems, run experiments, and are expected to have research judgment. Reinforcement learning, post-training
and large-scale training are named here far more than elsewhere. {{< var phd_research_engineer >}}% mention a
PhD, against {{< var phd_ai_engineer >}}% of AI engineer postings.

{{< include _gen/distinct_research-engineer.md >}}

</details>

## What interviews test beyond the posting {#loops}

A posting lists what the job needs; an interview loop tests a narrower, more standard set. The table below is
the usual structure of senior loops for these roles. It comes from how these loops are commonly run, not from
the posting text, so check each company's own interview guide.

| Round | MLE | AI engineer | Research engineer | Areas to review |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Coding (data structures and algorithms) | 1 or 2 rounds | 1 or 2 rounds, often practical: build a small service or agent | 1 round | [Software engineering](../skills/swe.qmd) |
| ML coding (implement a model, loss or training loop) | common | rare | very common | [Deep learning](../skills/dl.qmd), [ML fundamentals](../skills/mlfund.qmd) |
| ML breadth and depth | 1 round | lighter | 1 round, deeper on training | [ML fundamentals](../skills/mlfund.qmd), [Deep learning](../skills/dl.qmd), [LLM training](../skills/llm.qmd) |
| ML / AI system design | 1 round; ranking, retrieval or serving | 1 round; agent, RAG or eval system | sometimes; training or eval infrastructure | [Design cases](../skills/cases.qmd), [Search and recsys](../skills/recsys.qmd), [LLM applications](../skills/llmapp.qmd), [Inference](../skills/serving.qmd) |
| General system design | sometimes | common | sometimes | [Software engineering](../skills/swe.qmd), [MLOps](../skills/mlops.qmd) |
| Project deep dive | always | always | always, plus a paper or research discussion | [Senior scope](../skills/senior.qmd), [Research](../skills/research.qmd) |
| Behavioural and hiring manager | always | always; customer scenarios for forward-deployed roles | always; mission and safety questions at labs | [Senior scope](../skills/senior.qmd) |
| Take-home or work trial | sometimes | common at startups | sometimes | [Evaluation](../skills/eval.qmd), [LLM applications](../skills/llmapp.qmd) |

Two consequences for preparation. First, coding and behavioural rounds carry more weight than their share of
posting text suggests. Second, the design round is where the posting's skills are tested together, so the
[design cases](../skills/cases.qmd) are the best single place to practise them.

## Questions candidates report being asked {#reported}

The cards on this site were written from the skills the postings name. They were not copied from interviews.
To check them against practice, {{< var n_reports >}} questions that two third-party sites list as asked in
interviews at {{< var n_report_companies >}} employers from the sample were collected on
{{< var reports_retrieved >}}. Each is matched to the cards that cover its topic.

{{< include _gen/reported_summary.md >}}

{{< var n_reports_carded >}} of the reported questions are covered by {{< var n_reported_cards >}} cards.
Those cards carry an "asked at" tag on the [skill pages](../skills/index.qmd) and in the
[review app](../review/index.qmd), which can filter to them or run them as a mock round.
{{< var n_reports_nocard >}} reported questions have no card yet; they are listed below with their source so
they can be practised from there.

**How far to trust this.**

- The reports are self-submitted to those sites by candidates and are not verified here. PracHub describes
  its listings as real questions from candidate reports; Aced (formerly Exponent) is a user-contributed
  question bank plus first-person interview write-ups. Three entries are first-person write-ups; the rest are
  single listings.
- The topic column is a paraphrase. A card "covers" a report when it treats the same topic, not when it
  reproduces the question. Follow the link for the source's own wording.
- The sample is what was readable without an account. Glassdoor, 1Point3Acres and Blind hold more reports
  behind logins and were not used.
- Roles are as the source lists them and include some product manager and data scientist interviews, whose
  ML questions overlap with engineering ones.
- Interview questions change. Treat these as evidence about what kind of question is asked, not as a list
  to memorise.

**What the reports show.**

- *OpenAI, ML coding.* A small set of exercises recurs: debugging a small transformer with planted bugs and
  then adding a KV cache (10 of 68 reports), backpropagation by hand (6), a vectorised nearest-neighbour
  classifier (6), prefix products with their backward pass (4), and cleaning labels from noisy annotators
  (4). The design questions are mostly retrieval and enterprise search (10).
- *Anthropic.* 18 of 50 reports are inference-system design: batching, routing and scheduling on a GPU pool,
  and distributing model weights. Several others ask about safety and model behaviour.
- *Meta.* Recommendation, ranking and place recommendation (10 of 27) and integrity classifiers (5), with
  LLM system designs appearing in 2026.
- *Across employers.* Implementing attention is the single most reported coding task (11 reports at six
  employers). Behavioural questions are the standard ones: a mistake, a conflict, the project you are most
  proud of.

This agrees with the [interview loop table](#loops): coding and design carry the rounds, and the design
round tests the posting's skills together.

## Method and limits {#method}

**Counting.** Each skill has a set of text patterns (`tools/taxonomy.py`). Equal-opportunity, benefits and
company-boilerplate lines are removed before matching. A skill counts once per posting. The patterns were
checked against the phrases they match and tightened where a generic word inflated a count (for example
"reliable" or "integrations").

**What the share means.** It is how often employers write the skill down. It understates skills that are
assumed (Python, coding ability, statistics) and overstates words that are fashionable in posting language.
Treat differences of a few points as noise and read the ranking, the track differences and the large gaps.

**Sample.** The sample is the employers in the fetch list, not the whole market. It leans to AI labs, AI
startups and robotics, and to the United States. Employers that do not publish a machine-readable board are
missing unless `tools/fetch_jobs_bigtech.py` reaches them; the run log in `data/summary.json` records which
were fetched. Roles titled only "software engineer" or "research scientist" are outside the three tracks and
are not included.

**Level.** "Senior-eligible" means the title says senior, staff, lead or principal, or the title has no level
and the description does not ask for two years or less.

**Refreshing.** `python tools/fetch_jobs.py`, `python tools/fetch_jobs_bigtech.py`,
`python tools/analyze_skills.py`, then render the site. Postings are a snapshot; every number on this page
changes when the data is refreshed.
